items.originalTitle: Meet the 27-year old behind the protein ad that helped flip Mississippi
items.author: Erin Doherty
items.title: Meet the 27-year old behind the protein ad that helped flip Mississippi
items.summary: You know you’ve made a good ad when it’s outperforming an endorsement video from Barack Obama. Ryan Sayles, a 27-year-old Mississippi content creator, is behind arguably the best political spot of the election cycle: Democrat Scott Colom’s viral “ pick another protein ” ad against GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith. You’ve probably seen it by now. The ad featured Mississippi voters’ blunt reactions to Hyde-Smith’s suggestion that people struggling with rising beef prices choose from other protein options. “Pick another protein? Shiiii-, I’d rather pick another senator instead.” “Pick another protein? She done lost her damn mind. I’d rather pick another senator.” Sayles was at his nephew’s football game when he realized something extraordinary was happening. “I was looking at the first numbers when it first dropped, and I was like, ‘Oh, this is about to be a really good video,’” he told POLITICO after Colom’s historic Senate race victory in the longtime Republican stronghold. “We had the Obama endorsement the day before, so that was our biggest video. It was like, ‘Dang, we ain’t ever gonna top that.’” “And then this ad came, and we posted it, and it outperformed anything we ever did,” Sayles said. The 30-second spot quickly became the talk of Mississippi and Washington, helping fuel Colom’s longshot campaign to unseat Hyde-Smith and become the first Black senator from the state since Reconstruction. And, it’s given Democrats across the country another blueprint for how to break through online ahead of a critical 2028 presidential race, as the party continues to rethink its strategy. With the ad — and Colom’s win — Sayles has gone from a newcomer who stumbled into campaigning almost by accident to a name to watch in Democratic digital politics, as the party looks for fresh ways to reach voters ahead of 2028. “[Sayles] should be considered the breakout-star of this cycle,” Colom wrote in a post on X about the viral ad earlier this month. “He’s going to be a giant in the media consultant game. He did GAME CHANGING work with SO little.” In an interview with POLITICO, Sayles described how his lack of prior political experience shaped his approach to creating the ad and why he thinks Democrats should listen more closely to the voters they’re trying to reach. He also discussed the unexpected attention he’s received since the ad — and why he hopes Colom’s victory will serve as a wake-up call for the party to invest in the South. This interview has been edited for length and clarity. How did you get involved with the Colom campaign? I did a lot of freelance videography and photography, and they really just needed a photographer for one event they were doing back in October. And I came and did video and pictures for him, and they kept me around. They were like, "Yeah, we need to work with him,” and then from then on, I never left. Take me behind the scenes of creating the protein ad. How did it come together? Scott and his brother, Andrew, along with [the] campaign manager Gerard, they all plotted the script together, and so they presented it to me. We filmed it, and I directed and made sure it [felt] like Mississippi. I guess I made it more Mississippi than what it was at the beginning. You know, [I] just added the entertainment or funny pieces of it, like emphasizing the way he said the words and stuff like that. And then I shot it, edited it, and added the music to it. I sat there and edited for like five hours. I've heard that man say “shit” a million times. Did you think it was going to go this viral? I had high hopes for it, but I just didn't know what it could do. A lot of our content was getting around Mississippi, but it wasn't getting around the country. Mississippians knew about Scott Colom’s content and what he was doing, but it wasn't nationwide — and I think that ad really put a national focus on what was brewing in Mississippi. Why do you think this particular ad took off so much and felt so natural? I think the reason it did well nationally is because I think a lot of people are fed up. A lot of times we don't express the way we feel, we hold it in, but I think this ad was an expression that people felt all around the country, that we just had the guts to put it out there. For Mississippi, of course it resonated because that's something we say down here. People say “shiiiit” all the time — like you know, that's the normal conversation. I think the best thing about the ad was it was centering people, centering voters ... You know, Scott was in the ad for about five seconds, but then that was the biggest ad of the cycle. I think it was just a lesson that people matter way more than politics. Did anybody worry the ad went too far? Do you think Democrats are sometimes too cautious? I think the dope part is, we didn't run that ad by anybody. … We didn’t go around getting OK’s from anybody ... we just put it out. But also … I've never worked on a campaign, and I think that I didn't have a sense of what Dems normally did. You know what I mean? We just did what we liked, and that was one of the big things Scott always talked about. “Man, if we are good with the content, we are good.” Scott is the best person I could’ve been in this situation with. He has been such a great person. He’s so creative, and he has allowed me to shine in ways that I just can’t believe. Did you hear from people in the Democratic Party after the ad came out? Like I said, this is my first campaign, so this is all a blur right now, honestly. But I would say that I've gotten messages, a lot of messages. I don't know who all those messages are tied to at this point, but I have gotten a lot of messages and people saying, “You did great work, we should talk.” I'm just happy. Mississippi is, we have hope again, man, that's the biggest thing. You know, this is my state. What could the Democratic Party learn from the Colom campaign’s digital strategy? I want to shout out my digital director. Lacy Nelson was the digital director, and she really helped turn things around when it came to just our distribution being able to put stuff out, because at first I was posting, taking pictures, filming, editing, doing everything by myself, and it was the worst headache. You gotta put your feet on the ground, you gotta understand the area in which you are working to try to get voters, and you gotta let them know that you see them and make them feel seen. You have to understand what resonates with people. People in Mississippi are not going to care about the things that somebody who lives in New York City cares about, it's going to be different. And that messaging needs to be different. You can't give Mississippi a New York message. Not that I'm an expert — like I said, this is my first campaign — but I think people should really focus on what that region is listening to. What does Colom’s victory mean for Democrats’ opportunities across the South? For a long time we’ve looked at it as impossible. And with very little resources, we showed that if you really get out and you do the work, you talk to people, you meet voters where they are, it is possible. Mississippi is one of the hardest places that could have happened. When you look at the investment and you look at what other places have received for that type of thing, it shows that the opportunity was always in Mississippi. … We just needed the investment, and I think that over the years, so many organizations have done the work to get us to this point, and we just seized the opportunity. There's real opportunity in the South. You just gotta invest.

items.originalTitle: 2028 Dems: Don’t label me
items.author: Lisa Kashinsky
items.title: 2028 Dems: Don’t label me
items.summary: Democrats’ midterms sweep didn’t solve their ideological civil war — but a number of the party’s potential presidential contenders hope it lets them call a truce. In the days since Democrats’ sweeping midterm victories, several likely White House aspirants have argued that their party’s factional feuding needs to take a backseat heading into 2028. “What was clear, no matter where you go, [is that] people are frustrated,” Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro told reporters last weekend at Crooked Media’s post-election conference. “They're not thinking about whether this is about left or middle or right. They're thinking about how to get problems solved.” “I don't know if the takeaway should be what ideology that people wanted. I think people want results,” Maryland Gov. Wes Moore said at the same event. Democrats’ midterm tidal wave was powered more by voters’ anger at high costs and the Trump administration than by any one ideology. Candidates won tough races by positioning themselves not as progressives or moderates but as anti-Washington populists and pragmatists — some of them even scoring dual endorsements from both the moderate Blue Dog Democrats and progressive Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.). “If you see … an elected leader spending valuable time duking it out on whose team won, moderate or progressive, they are missing the actual message of this election,” Michigan Sen. Elissa Slotkin, a moderate who campaigned hard for progressive Abdul El-Sayed, told POLITICO. “It’s about people who are wanting to work together as a team on issues like the American dream in the middle class.”Many of the party’s rising stars embraced an ethos like Shapiro’s “get stuff done” and, like Slotkin, called to reject progressive-versus-moderate politics in favor of combative candidates. “It helps take away the most annoying question that has split our party, and that is the question of electability,” progressive Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) said in an interview last week. “It turns out that progressives were electable, and centrists were electable. The moderates were electable, and people who were affiliated with the DSA were electable.” Now, as they pivot into 2028, Democrats are broadly seizing on last week’s results as license to avoid traditional labels as they look to appeal as widely as possible to voters more interested in easing the pinch in their pocketbooks than the political philosophy to which their leaders subscribe. Interviews and conversations with more than a dozen potential Democratic presidential candidates, advisers and operatives reveal that rhetorical shift is as much a rejection of the ideological litmus tests that dominated the 2020 primary as it is a calibration toward the dynamics that will drive the 2028 contest. “We all lived through the purity tests,” said Adrienne Elrod, a Democratic strategist who advised Joe Biden in 2020, Kamala Harris in 2024 and Hillary Clinton’s 2016 run. “What people are now yearning for is authenticity. And they want a fighter and someone who can deliver more than someone who perfectly aligns with them ideologically.” There are tells in the flurry of postelection memos from potential presidential contenders. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez’s team positioned her not as a progressive firebrand but as “one of the most effective voices in the country for America’s working class.” Teams behind Moore and Shapiro pushed messages of “common-sense governance” and “delivering results.” “There has been a reckoning in the Democratic Party, and people in all lanes frankly have come to realize the government in Washington has not delivered for working-class people and they need to,” said Jeff Weaver, a Khanna adviser who managed Sanders’ 2016 presidential campaign. Or, as one adviser to a potential candidate said: Voters “do not live in the binaries that a lot of political operatives do.” While last Tuesday’s wave swept Democrats of all stripes into office, it also created openings for each wing of the party to argue that its vision is the way forward. That all but guarantees more proxy battles to come as the party moves from running a raft of candidates across diverse districts to selecting just one to try and win the White House. The left has seized on strong performances by unabashedly progressive candidates to push Khanna and Ocasio-Cortez to run for president and Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) to challenge Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) for Senate majority leader. Ravi Mangla, a spokesperson for the Working Families Party, said it’s “undeniable the populist candidates … can win in swing states that are going to be critical in 2028” — and the left lane is “wide open.” But the centrist group Welcome argued in a new memo shared first with POLITICO that there’s a clear pathway for candidates willing to embrace a more moderate posture. “In a very large field, you need a base to get you to 15, 20, 25 percent. And it’s very clear in the data you can get there with voters in the middle — center-left voters,” said Welcome co-founder Liam Kerr. And even as he called for a primary that would battle test a diverse set of ideological views, Khanna, who co-chaired Sanders’ 2020 campaign, leaned into his liberal bona fides: “It would be an honor to be called a Bernie Sanders Democrat; I embrace being a New Deal Democrat with pride.” “Obviously, I'm a progressive Democrat. I believe that the progressive vision is the best vision. But there should be someone who’s in the center or center-left. Then they can argue for their vision,” Khanna said. “And then it’s for the American people and the primary to decide.” A version of this article first appeared in POLITICO Pro’s Morning Score.
